ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: In the image there is a large regular hexagon, with a smaller regular hexagon inside, and the surroundings are divided by four quadrilaterals; among them, two quadrilaterals are colored dark, and the other two are not colored. According to the regular hexagon structure and symmetry in the figure, the total area of the two dark pieces is the same as the total area of the two light-colored pieces, so in the large regular hexagon, the total area outside the small regular hexagon is 2 times the area of the dark part. Let the area of the small hexagon be S, and the area of the dark part be D. The problem gives D/S = 4/3, so D = 4S/3. Thus the total area of the external quadrilaterals = 2D = 8S/3. The area of the large hexagon = S + 8S/3 = 11S/3, therefore S/area of the large hexagon = S/(11S/3) = 3/11.

method.method_draft: First inspect the diagram: the big regular hexagon is partitioned into a smaller regular hexagon plus four surrounding quadrilaterals. Two of those quadrilaterals are shaded dark and two are unshaded. By the symmetry/regularity shown in the diagram, the shaded pair has the same combined area as the unshaded pair, so the total area outside the small hexagon is twice the area of the dark sections. Let the small hexagon area be S and the dark area be D. The text gives D/S = 4/3, so D = 4S/3. Therefore the total outer quadrilateral area is 2D = 8S/3. The big hexagon area is S + 8S/3 = 11S/3. Hence S/(big hexagon area) = S/(11S/3) = 3/11.
